processing: Darjeeling orthodox black tea from a garden with its own factory, grown under certified organic and biodynamic methods since 1992.
harvest_season: As with other Darjeeling gardens, first flush in early spring and second flush in early summer are the most prized.
appearance_dry: Twisted leaf in the usual Darjeeling mix, greener in spring and browner in summer.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold to amber depending on the flush, as is typical of Darjeeling.
taste_profile: As with other Darjeelings, expect floral and brisk first flush teas and rounder, fruitier second flush ones; little is recorded about this garden's own signature.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Cooler water for first flush; a touch hotter for summer lots.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush with a lot or invoice number, as is usual in Darjeeling. First flush arrives first and costs more, and these teas are at their best within a year or two. Check the harvest year on the packet rather than the estate name alone.
description:
Ambootia sits below Kurseong and is one of the better known Darjeeling gardens, partly for its size and partly for its early move to organic and biodynamic farming. It is a sizeable place: 790 hectares in total with 350 under tea.

The garden has its own factory, and growing methods are what set it apart. Certification came in 1992, Fair Trade in 1994.

Little is recorded about a house style, so judge each lot on its flush. As is typical of Darjeeling, spring teas want gentler water and summer teas can take more. Do not brew either until it is bitter.

Buy by year and flush. The name also once stood for a much larger group of gardens, so a tea sold as Ambootia may not always mean this very garden; ask if it matters to you.
history:
Accounts date the garden to the British planting era: it is described as one of the first established in the 1850s, and also as set up by the Darjeeling Tea Company of England in 1861. It passed to Indian owners in 1954, and was a declared sick unit by the time the Bansal Tea Group took over in 1987.

A landslide in October 1968 scarred the area and stayed active until re-vegetation began to stabilise it in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Under the Ambootia group the estate became a known organic name, and the group grew to hold 12 Darjeeling gardens.

After financial distress, the garden and five others were handed over in late 2022 to Lemongrass Organic Tea Estates.
